chapter_theme: Rebuked by a deity and pursued by his own desire, the prince withdraws; Manimekalai, to escape him, takes Kayachandigai's form and feeds the king's prisoners from the bowl, and while the king plays in his grove the guard reports her, and at her request he turns the prison into a house of dharma.

cast.role: the Chola king's son, who desires Manimekalai
a deity speaking from a crafted image in the old goddess's shrine, who rebukes the prince
the young men of the city playing lutes with their women at nightfall
Madhavi's daughter, here in Kayachandigai's form
the guards of the king's prison, one of whom reports to the king
the Chola king of Puhar, Udayakumaran's father
the Chola queen, Udayakumaran's mother, of Mavali's line
the women skilled in dance, music and adornment who sport with the king
the craftsmen of Magadha, Maratha, Avanti, the Yavanas and the Tamil land who built the pavilion

manimekalai:19:1-28.unit_note: Boundary moved from 16/17 to 28/29: line 16 ('பின் அறிவாம்' எனப் பெயர்வோன் தன்னை) leaves the prince as the object of a sentence that ends only at line 28 (அவன் போய பின்).
manimekalai:19:1-28.reading: After the prince bows three times at the old goddess's feet and swears his vow, a deity in a crafted image rebukes him for speaking rashly before 'our lady'; shaken, he counts three wonders (the deity who showed him the sceptre and told him to forget her, the bowl she carries to end many people's hunger, and the image's charge that he wronged the 'first lady' of old) and resolves to learn their meaning from the girl's later deeds, and he goes off as evening, pictured as a riderless musth elephant with the crescent for its tusk, hounds him and the city youths' lute music tears his heart.
manimekalai:19:1-28.nuance: Whom the image means by எம் கோமகள் (3) and முத்தை முதல்வி (13) is not settled by this unit: the old goddess of the shrine, or Manimekalai as his wife of a former birth (kaathai 10 told her the prince was Rahulan). The prince does not yield; he defers (பின் அறிவாம், 16). Evening comes 'with an aspect that destroys restraint' (நிறை அழி தோற்றமொடு, 23), so the loss of nirai is cast as something that pursues him from outside.
manimekalai:19:1-28.event: Rebuked by a deity speaking from a crafted image, Udayakumaran, shaken, decides to learn more from the girl's deeds and leaves the shrine at nightfall in torment.

manimekalai:19:29-50.unit_note: Boundary moved from 49/50 to 50/51: the guards' words begun at 48 (கோமகன் தனக்கு இப் பாத்திர தானமும் பைந்தொடி செய்தியும்) end only at line 50 (இசைத்தும்' என்று ஏகி).
manimekalai:19:29-50.reading: Inside the shrine's chamber Manimekalai reasons that if she goes about the hall as Madhavi's daughter the prince will not let her be, so she takes the form of Kayachandigai, known to the whole city as a woman of burning hunger, citing the learned that for an alms-seeker taking and giving are both duty but going to the needy to give is the finer thing; she takes the Amudhasurabhi from the goddess's shrine, enters the king's prison for those who offended him, and with a sigh feeds the hungry there until her hand aches, and the guards, marvelling that one bowl fed them all, go to report the gift and the girl to the king.
manimekalai:19:29-50.nuance: The disguise has two motives in one breath: to escape the prince (31-32) and to serve the helpless (35). Kayachandigai's known insatiable hunger makes the borrowed body a fitting carrier for a bowl that never empties. She enters the prison 'with desire' (விருப்பொடும், 44): the prison is chosen, not stumbled on.
manimekalai:19:29-50.event: Manimekalai takes Kayachandigai's form, carries the bowl into the king's prison and feeds the prisoners, and the guards go to tell the king.

claims.claim: for one who lives on alms, both receiving and giving are duties, and going out to the needy to give is the higher act

manimekalai:19:51-66.unit_note: Boundary moved from 65/66 to 66/67: line 65 opens the king's exclamation ('மாமணி வண்ணனும் தம்முனும் பிஞ்ஞையும்) and line 66 closes it (ஆடிய குரவை இஃது ஆம்' என நோக்கியும்).
manimekalai:19:51-66.reading: Meanwhile the king, with Queen Seerthi, daughter of the line of Mavali who poured the gift-water when the tall god took a dwarf's form and measured the earth, enters a flowering grove where bees, beetles, koels and peacocks make a concert, and seeing peahens, peacocks and a mateless swan whirl together he says it is the kuravai that the gem-coloured god, his elder brother and Pinnai danced.
manimekalai:19:51-66.nuance: The queen's line is traced to Mavali, the king who lost the earth by his gift to the dwarf, while the king amuses himself; the grove scene runs alongside Manimekalai's prison feeding, which the guards are on their way to report.
manimekalai:19:51-66.event: The Chola king enters a pleasure grove with his queen and reads the birds' whirling as the divine kuravai.

manimekalai:19:67-78.unit_note: Boundary moved from 77/78 to 78/79: line 77 (நெடியோன் முன்னொடு நின்றனன் ஆம் என) is completed by line 78 (தொழுது நின்று ஏத்தியும்).
manimekalai:19:67-78.reading: The king goes on finding pictures in the grove: a peacock beside a mango and kongu blossom is a doll feeding milk from a gold plate to a parrot, a male monkey swinging a female on the jewelled swing made for women makes him laugh, and green bamboo standing by white-flowered maraam is the tall god standing with his elder brother, to which he joins bangled hands in worship.
manimekalai:19:67-78.nuance: The bangled hand (தொடி சேர் செங் கை, 78) could be the queen's, but the run of participles (நோக்கியும், நகை எய்தியும், ஏத்தியும்) keeps the king as subject.
manimekalai:19:67-78.event: The king sees likenesses in the grove, laughs at the monkeys on the swing and worships a bamboo and maraam pair as Krishna and his brother.

manimekalai:19:79-92.unit_note: Boundary moved from 93/94 (unit 78-93) to 92/93: line 92 (வேந்தனின் சென்று விளையாட்டு அயர்ந்து) closes the clause of the women and their sport; line 93 begins the flowering shrubs.
manimekalai:19:79-92.reading: With women who know dance and gesture, who know the drama-poems, set the modes on the lute, beat the drum, keep time with flute and voice, string pearls, rub on sandal, paint saffron on their breasts, braid lilies, perfume their hair and stand before golden mirrors, the king plays like the king of the wide sky.
manimekalai:19:79-92.event: The king sports in the grove with women skilled in dance, music and adornment.

manimekalai:19:93-106.unit_note: Boundary moved from 108/109 (unit 94-108) to 106/107: line 106 (யாங்கணும் திரிந்து தாழ்ந்து விளையாடி) ends the king's wandering; line 107 begins the craftsmen who built the pavilion.
manimekalai:19:93-106.reading: Standing among kurunthu, jasmine and other shrubs, the king smiles and calls a mongoose, a hare, a leaping deer and a lurking creature to come, beckoning with his hand beside his beloved companion, and with Kama, spring and the young south wind as his fellows he wanders and plays among machine-wells, built hills, falls, ponds, hidden pools, hiding places and crystal chambers.
manimekalai:19:93-106.nuance: Kama, spring and the breeze are named as the king's companions (100-101), so the king's play is drawn as a festival of desire at the hour his son is being turned back by a goddess.
manimekalai:19:93-106.event: The king plays with animals and wanders through the grove's artificial wells, hills, pools and crystal rooms.

manimekalai:19:107-116.unit_note: New unit from the redrawn 109-127: it begins at 107 where the craftsmen enter and ends at 116 (இனிது ஏறலும), where the king's long sentence of play closes before the guard's approach at 117.
manimekalai:19:107-116.reading: The king, Indra-like, mounts a pavilion of green gold that Magadha artisans, Maratha smiths, Avanti metalworkers and Yavana carpenters made with Tamil craftsmen, with coral pillars, jewelled capitals, hanging strings of pearl and a gold-sheathed canopy.
manimekalai:19:107-116.nuance: The list of foreign craftsmen working with Tamil ones (107-109) is a picture of Puhar's reach through trade.
manimekalai:19:107-116.event: The king ascends the golden pavilion built by craftsmen from many lands.

manimekalai:19:117-138.unit_note: The original units 109-127 and 128-143 were redrawn as 107-116, 117-138 and 139-162: line 117 (வாயிலுக்கு இசைத்து) begins the guard's approach, and line 138 (வாழி எம் கோ மன்னவ!' என்றலும்) ends his speech.
manimekalai:19:117-138.reading: Announced at the gate and admitted by the king's grace, the prison guard bows and praises Maavankilli, whose protecting umbrella was won at Kaariyaaru by the young prince over the bow-and-fish banners that came out of Vanji wearing the vanji flower in hunger for land, and then reports that a stranger woman, wasted by the elephant-fire disease, entered the prison, blessed the king's name, and with one begging bowl made food flow for the crowding prisoners.
manimekalai:19:117-138.nuance: The bow and fish of 124 are the Chera and Pandya emblems, so the enemies who came from Vanji appear to be their alliance; whether the young prince (இளங்கோன், 125) is Udayakumaran is not said. The guard frames the prisoners' feeding as a blessing on the king's name (134), before the king has done anything.
manimekalai:19:117-138.event: The prison guard is admitted, praises the king's victory at Kaariyaaru and reports the stranger woman who feeds the prisoners from one bowl.

manimekalai:19:139-162.unit_note: Boundary moved from 143/144 to 138/139: the king's question begins at 143 (தவத்தோய் நீ யார்?) and ends at 144 (என்று), so the dialogue is kept whole from the king's summons at 139.
manimekalai:19:139-162.reading: The king graciously summons her; she comes and blesses him, and asked who she is and how she came by the bowl, she says she is a vidyadhara woman who has wandered the festive old city in disguise, blesses rain, earth and the prince, and says a deity near the hall gave the bowl, which became divine, ended her elephant-fire hunger and is life-medicine for embodied beings; when the king asks what he should do for her, she asks him to clear the prison and make it a house for those who do dharma, and he releases the prisoners and makes the prison into such a house.
manimekalai:19:139-162.nuance: Her self-account is true and false at once: she calls herself a vidyadhara woman (விஞ்சை மகள், 147), which is Kayachandigai's identity, while saying she has wandered the city in வஞ்சம் (148), which names her disguise. Her blessing 'no harm to the prince' (150) comes just before the prince is killed because of that disguise. The king does not punish or pardon one offender; he abolishes the prison as an institution at a beggar's request. Line 160 (through the great ascetics, great wealth gained) is compressed: whether the ascetics are given the building, or the king gains merit through them, is not clear.
manimekalai:19:139-162.event: Manimekalai, in Kayachandigai's form, tells the king of the bowl and asks him to turn the prison into a house of dharma, and he frees the prisoners and does so.

claims.claim: a king should clear his prison and give it over, with compassion, to those who practise dharma

links.note: In the grove the prince asked whether any restraint holds once desire takes root; here evening pursues him 'with an aspect that destroys restraint' and he leaves burning and sighing.
links.teaches: The prince's line that no நிறை survives rooted desire was his licence to pursue; two kaathais on, the same loss of restraint is drawn as a beast that hounds him away from her, so his excuse becomes his torment.

links.note: The goddess gave her a mantra to take another form and travel the sky so that no one would refuse her teaching for her youth; here she first uses the other form to evade the prince and enter a prison with the bowl.
links.teaches: The power given so she could hear doctrine as an adult is first spent on escaping desire and feeding prisoners, so the epic puts charity and self-protection before debate in the order of her training.

links.note: The patikam tells that Kanchanan, taking her for Kayachandigai, approached her and killed the prince; here she chooses that form to keep the prince away.
links.teaches: The disguise she takes to be free of Udayakumaran is what brings Kayachandigai's husband upon him, so her flight from the prince is the cause of his death, which the patikam names and this kaathai does not yet show.

links.note: The couplet calls taking bad even if it were a good path and giving good even without heaven; Manimekalai cites the learned that for an alms-seeker both taking and giving are duty, and going to give is better still.
links.teaches: The couplet's flat ranking of giving over taking leaves no place for the mendicant, while the epic makes taking a duty when it serves giving, so the beggar's bowl is let in under the couplet's rule rather than condemned by it.

gains.a: Her maxim gains a sharp statement of the view it must answer: that taking is bad whatever the path.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case it does not cover, the one who takes only in order to give.

links.note: The herdswomen dance the kuravai of Mayavan, his elder brother and Pinnai to ward off the omens before Kovalan's death; the Chola king sees that same kuravai in birds whirling in his pleasure grove.
links.teaches: Across the two epics the one divine dance is first a rite of fear performed by herdswomen over coming disaster and then a pleasantry of a king at play, while Kovalan's daughter works in his prison, so the image measures how far the court stands from the suffering it governs.

links.note: The quatrain's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) fills slowly by alms at door after door; the guard reports a begging bowl (ஐயப் பாத்திரம்) that, taken into the prison, makes food flow for a crowd.
links.teaches: The quatrain uses the begging bowl as the image of slow accumulation in the giver, and the epic reverses its direction, making the ascetic's bowl the source that pours out, so in the Buddhist epic the mendicant is the giver and the city the receiver.

gains.a: The marvel of the one bowl gains the ordinary picture of a begging bowl it overturns.
gains.b: The quatrain's image gains a counter-case where the bowl's fullness belongs to the beggar, not the donor.

links.note: The couplet likens a king's punishing the cruel to weeding a crop; the Chola king, at a beggar's request, empties his prison and makes it a house of dharma.
links.teaches: Held against the couplet, the epic's king does not deny that the cruel must be punished but turns the instrument of punishment itself into an instrument of charity, so the sceptre is shown by feeding rather than weeding.

gains.a: The king's act gains the standard view of royal punishment it departs from.
gains.b: The couplet's weeding image gains a royal alternative it does not consider, in which the prison is abolished rather than filled.

links.note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that those who give food give life and urges him to build tanks; the disguised girl tells the Chola her bowl is life-medicine for embodied beings and asks him to give the prison to the righteous.
links.teaches: Both poems set a counsellor before a king to teach that feeding is giving life, but the Sangam poet asks for waterworks that bring fame and the other world, while the epic's beggar asks the king to give up a prison, so the duty to feed passes from royal works to a renouncer's bowl the king only endorses.

gains.a: The girl's plea gains a Tamil royal precedent for the claim that food is life.
gains.b: The poem's counsel gains a later scene where the one who feeds is not the king, which shifts who holds the life-giving power.

links.note: Aravanar called the Amudhasurabhi life-medicine (ஆர் உயிர் மருந்து) and said many events would come to the city through her; she tells the king the bowl is life-medicine (உயிர் மருந்து) and the prison becomes a house of dharma.
links.teaches: Her words to the king repeat her teacher's phrase, and her first public act fulfils his prophecy of events in the city, so the epic shows the teaching passing into civic change through the disciple's voice before she has formally taken the dharma.

new_concepts.gloss: the prison, the king's house of punishment for those who offend him
new_concepts.label_source: The text's word: சிறைக்கோட்டம் (43, 133), சிறையோர் கோட்டம் (157, 161), அருஞ் சிறை (159)

source_issues: Line 63 reads இரு சிறைக் விரித்து, with a doubled க் before வி; line 64 has the expected ஒரு சிறைக் கண்டு. Probably இரு சிறை விரித்து.
Line 109 reads வினைஞ்அர், a typing error for வினைஞர்.
Line 1 opens mid-scene: முதியாள் and the prince's வஞ்சினம் continue the previous kaathai.
Quotation marks are unbalanced: line 3 opens a single quote, line 9 a double, and line 16 closes with a single quote after அறிவாம்.
Line 162 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle.

Unit boundaries at 16/17 (break score 0), 49/50, 65/66, 77/78, 93/94, 108/109, 127/128 and 143/144 fell inside sentences or speeches; the chapter was recut into nine units: 1-28, 29-50, 51-66, 67-78, 79-92, 93-106, 107-116, 117-138, 139-162.
